outputs.L3:
There is a particular kind of solace that arrives unexpectedly, and for me it comes in the form of a massive pair of eagles sweeping just above the roofline of my house. Their sudden appearance cuts through the bitterness I have been carrying—the bitterness that accumulates from witnessing so much damage in the landscape around me. Where I might otherwise be consumed by anger and grief, the sight of those great wings arrests everything, and for a moment the resentment loosens its grip.

Yet not every clarity brings relief. On a clear blue morning, when the air is sharp and every detail stands out with uncommon precision, I have discovered that this heightened clarity does not comfort me at all. Instead, it intensifies my pain. The very brightness that should feel like a gift becomes a magnifying lens, forcing me to see too much, too vividly, until the beauty itself becomes almost unbearable.

My sensitivity to this place runs so deep that the loss of even a single small wattle tree can bring me profound agony. It is not a measured, reasonable sorrow but something visceral—a feeling of being close to death, of struggling to breathe, of being unable to function. One vanished tree, insignificant to most, can undo me entirely, as though a part of my own body has been cut away.

I have come to understand that I perceive my home region through a kind of internal compass. Rather than taking in the whole landscape evenly, my attention is continually drawn toward one particular spot—a place I have observed so closely and cherished so completely that it orients everything else. All my awareness bends toward it, as a needle turns steadily to north.

And so I return to the eagles. I know, watching them, that they are predators, that their grace conceals violence, that they inflict traumatic harm upon whatever prey they seize. I do not pretend otherwise. Yet even with this knowledge, the simple act of watching them overrides my emotional ordeal. Whatever anguish I carry is momentarily suspended, held at bay by the sheer force of their presence overhead.
outputs.L4:
# Solace in Flight: Nature's Fragile Consolation

The poem opens a window into a deeply personal encounter with the natural world, one where beauty and loss exist in uneasy proximity. At its heart lies a moment of witnessing—the speaker observes a magnificent pair of eagles soaring high above their home, their effortless grace cutting through the sky in wide, commanding arcs. This image becomes the emotional fulcrum around which the entire piece turns.

Against the splendor of these birds, the poem sets a quieter but no less profound sorrow: the grief born of environmental loss. Remarkably, this pain is not expressed through catastrophic scenes of widespread destruction, but through something far more intimate—the agony felt over a single vanished wattle tree. This deliberate narrowing of focus intensifies the emotional weight. The absence of one tree becomes a lens through which the larger tragedy of ecological decline is understood, suggesting that grief for the natural world can be triggered by the smallest of losses, each one carrying disproportionate significance.

Through vivid imagery, the poem draws these two forces into sharp relief. The eagles, powerful and alive, embody survival and continuity; the missing wattle represents everything that has been diminished, erased, or forgotten. In their juxtaposition, the poem reveals a central truth: natural beauty can offer solace, but that solace is fragile. The sight of the eagles does not erase the pain—it exists alongside it, a temporary counterweight rather than a cure.

This tension forms the emotional core of the work. The speaker is caught between two contradictory experiences: the trauma of witnessing environmental destruction and the meaning found in whatever endures. There is comfort in the eagles' survival, yet that comfort is shadowed by an awareness of how much has already been lost, and how easily beauty itself might disappear.

Ultimately, the poem resists offering easy consolation. Instead, it dwells honestly in the complexity of loving a world that is being damaged—acknowledging that moments of natural beauty can steady the grieving heart, even as they remind us of the fragility of all we hold dear. In doing so, it captures the delicate, often painful balance between mourning what is gone and cherishing what remains.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in one long, run-on sentence about seeing a pair of eagles over your rural home and how it counteracts grief over environmental loss.
counterfactuals.output:
Because this morning when I stepped out barefoot onto the cold porch boards
still holding the grief I've carried like a stone swallowed years ago,
the grief of vanished creeks gone to culvert and concrete,
of the meadow behind the Hendersons' now a hundred vinyl houses,
of the frogs I no longer hear in April, of the monarchs
thinning to a rumor, of the newspapers folded to headlines
I can barely read anymore for the ache of them,
there they were, two eagles, riding the thermals over the barn,
turning those slow deliberate circles that ask nothing and promise nothing
and yet somehow, in the white flare of their heads against the gray,
in the way the larger one tucked and dropped and the other followed,
in that ancient uncomplicated fact of them being alive
above my crooked fence and my failing garden and my small human sorrow,
something loosened in my chest, not hope exactly, not the naive kind
that ignores what we have broken, but something stubborn and feathered
that says here, still here, despite the poison years, despite the near-erasure,
banking now toward the ridge where the pines still stand,
and I stood watching until my neck ached and the coffee went cold in my hands,
grateful past speaking that the world had kept back this one wild pair
to remind me the story is not finished,
that grief and wonder can share the same wide sky,
and that as long as anything so fierce and free still wheels above these hills,
I am not permitted to stop loving what remains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem in the style of John Kinsella, exploring bitterness, loss of a wattle tree, and the sight of eagles above the house.
counterfactuals.output:
**Loss of the Wattle, with Eagles**

It went the way most things go here—
quietly, then all at once, the acacia
that seeded itself against my wishes
and became, against my wishes, necessary.
Root-rot or the dry, or both conspiring,
the way conspiracy is just weather
with a longer memory. Its yellow
was a currency I hadn't known I'd banked.

Now the space it kept is only space,
a gap the wind moves through without
comment, and I am bitter—yes, I'll say it—
bitter as the resin that wept where the branch
came down, bitter as the taste
of having warned no one, having warned
only the tree, which does not listen,
which is the whole grief of it.

But look: two wedge-tailed eagles
riding the thermal off the shed's tin heat,
so high they are almost the idea of eagles,
the wing-fingers spread, the tilt
that costs them nothing and reads
the invisible column like scripture.
They do not mourn the wattle.
They mourn nothing. They are the argument
against my mourning, and also its proof—

that something still climbs the ruined air,
that the paddock's cleared insult
is only the ground they measure from,
that bitterness is a low thing,
a thing of the root-zone, the wet dark,
while overhead the raptors turn
and turn, indifferent, exact,
holding the whole diminished country
in the slow wheel of their looking.

I go inside. The stump stays.
The eagles keep their height
above the house like a verdict
I am not yet ready to translate.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**Homecoming, October**

the gravel same the mailbox same the bend

where was the oak the one I climbed

gone the way things go the way the light
comes in now unforgiving crisp
this air could cut you this blue could
and there them there against it

the wind that used to comb those branches

and I stand in the driveway keys still cold

and think how a thing can be here your whole

the eagles don't care the eagles have

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary Australian ecopoem where the speaker reflects on environmental damage, a personal sense of direction, and finds solace in watching eagles despite feeling their prey's pain too.
counterfactuals.output:
**Wedge-tail Compass**

I have lost the true north in me.
The paddocks my grandfather cleared
still smoke each summer, a red argument
between the sky and what we took from it—
the box-gum ironbark gone to fenceposts,
the creek a memory pencilled in cracked mud.

I drive the highway past the dieback,
the corridor of stumps like broken teeth,
and I cannot say which way is forward.
The satnav insists. I don't believe it.
The country I was promised as a boy
keeps subtracting itself from the map.

But there—above the granite tor,
a wedge-tail rides the thermals up,
her fingered wings spread wide as doubt,
and I pull over just to watch her hang,
motionless in the moving air,
certain of an axis I have mislaid.

She reads the land the way I can't,
each ridge and thermal, each small heat
rising off the sun-struck stone.
She is the one true compass left,
turning slow above the ruined green,
and something in me steadies, lifts.

Then she folds. Drops like a thrown stone.
And in the grass a rabbit's final cry
enters me, becomes my own—
that flare of terror, warm and quick,
the small heart stopped inside her grip.
I feel it. Both of them. I feel it all.

This is the bargain I keep learning:
you cannot love the hunter's clean arc
without the dying underneath it,
cannot praise the living balance
without holding, in your two cupped hands,
the weight of what is always paid.

So I stand beside the fenceline, grieving,
grateful, lost, and found, and lost—
watching her lift the ruined air to grace
above the country we have wounded,
her shadow crossing all of it,
naming a direction I might follow home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about how witnessing something majestic in nature can override deep grief, using imagery of eagles, tin roofing, and a vanished tree.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Eagle Over the Empty Place**

I came to where the elm had stood,
to grieve the absence, root and crown—
that green cathedral of my childhood
the winter storms had taken down.

Only the stump remained, a wound
gone gray with weather, ringed with rain,
and I stood there, my own heart pruned,
counting the years like counting pain.

The old barn leaned against the sky,
its tin roof buckled, silver-bright,
and I had come there just to cry
beneath that vacancy of light—

when something crossed the noon. A shadow
poured across the ruined tin,
and every rivet, nail, and furrow
flared as the great bird wheeled in.

An eagle, riding on the burning
plane of afternoon, so near
I heard the wind through pinions turning—
and grief went quiet, stunned to hear.

It did not need the tree to land on.
It did not mourn the missing shade.
It held the whole blue air, abandoned
to nothing that the storm had made.

And for that moment I forgot
the ache I'd carried like a stone—
the roof, the bird, the empty spot
all lifted, and I was not alone.

The eagle did not stay. It slid
back into distance, gold and gone.
But something in me, long since hid,
had glimpsed the reason to go on:

that even where the tree is vanished,
even above the broken shed,
some vast and shining thing, unbanished,
still climbs the light. And I was led—

not out of grief, but through its center,
the way the eagle cleaves the air,
to know the world can still enter
a heart that thought it only bore

the shape of loss. The tin cooled slowly.
The stump kept still its silent rings.
But I walked home beneath the holy,
wide, indifferent mercy of wings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
